extracted.intended_audience: readers with a modest undergraduate mathematics background (undergraduate students, mathematically inclined readers interested in elegant proofs)
extracted.subtask_description: Presenting and explaining elementary-but-brilliant ("Book") proofs of classical results in number theory, combinatorics, geometry, and analysis, accessible to readers with modest undergraduate preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes a 'Proof from The Book'
rubrics_metrics.description: No formal definition is given; selection is based on examples the authors selected, influenced strongly by Paul Erdős, intended to reflect "brilliant ideas, clever insights and wonderful observations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors state: "We have no definition or characterization of what constitutes a proof from The Book: all we offer here is the examples that we have selected, hoping that our readers will share our enthusiasm about brilliant ideas, clever insights and wonderful observations." The selection is influenced by Erdős, and many proofs trace directly back to him or were initiated by his questions/conjectures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Material is chosen to be accessible to readers whose backgrounds include only a modest amount of undergraduate mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically: "A little linear algebra, some basic analysis and number theory, and a healthy dollop of elementary concepts and reasonings from discrete mathematics should be sufficient to understand and enjoy everything in this book." This is a production/audience requirement for which proofs are selected and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common basic proof strategy for infinitude of primes
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that natural numbers grow without bound and that every n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor; these two facts combined force the set of primes to be infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors note: "Although they use different view-points, the following basic idea is common to all of them: The natural numbers grow beyond all bounds, and every natural number n ≥ 2 has a prime divisor. These two facts taken together force P to be infinite." This is a high-level desideratum for proofs of infinitude of primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclid-style constructive contradiction (product + 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any finite set of primes {p1,...,pr}, consider n = p1p2···pr + 1; any prime divisor of n is new, contradicting finiteness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic and canonical method for proving infinitude of primes; presented verbatim as "For any finite set {p1,...,pr} of primes, consider the number n = p1p2···pr + 1." Use: produce a number with a prime factor not in the assumed finite list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat-number recursion / pairwise coprimality technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Fermat numbers Fn = 22^n + 1 and the recursion product_{k=0}^{n-1} Fk = Fn - 2 to show distinctness (pairwise coprimality) of Fermat numbers; hence infinitely many primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove the recursion by induction and conclude that any two Fermat numbers are relatively prime (so each introduces new prime divisors). Example Fermat numbers listed: F0 = 3, F1 = 5, F2 = 17, F3 = 257, F4 = 65537, F5 = 641*6700417.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group-theoretic order argument (Lagrange) in primality proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Lagrange's theorem: in a finite multiplicative group, the order of any element divides the group size; applied to Z_q^× to deduce existence of larger primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied in the Mersenne-number proof: if q divides 2^p - 1 then order of 2 in Z_q^× is p, so p divides q-1 and hence q > p. The boxed statement: 'If G is a finite (multiplicative) group and U is a subgroup, then |U| divides |G|.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparing sums and integrals for estimates (harmonic/log comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate sums like harmonic numbers by integrals of 1/t to obtain log bounds (e.g., log x compared with sums of 1/m over m ≤ x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in the 'Fourth Proof' of infinitude of primes: compare area under f(t)=1/t with step functions to derive bounds log x ≤ sum_{m with prime divisors ≤ x} 1/m etc., leading to π(x) unbounded. Appendix explains method: H_n ≈ log n and more precise expansions with Euler's constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological construction using arithmetic progressions (Fürstenberg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a topology on Z whose basic open sets are arithmetic progressions N_{a,b} = {a + nb : n ∈ Z}; deduce properties of openness/closedness to force infinitude of primes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key facts: any nonempty open set is infinite; each N_{a,b} is closed as well; Z \ {±1} = ⋃_{p∈P} N_{0,p}. If P were finite, union of finitely many closed sets would be closed, making {±1} open, contradicting first fact. This is a methodological rubric: recast number-theoretic statements as topological properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős combinatorial divergence argument for sum_{p} 1/p
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition primes into 'small' (first k) and 'big' (rest) so that tail sum of reciprocals < 1/2; for N estimate count of integers ≤ N divisible by big primes and those with only small prime divisors to reach a contradiction if sum converged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define Nb = count of n ≤ N divisible by some big prime, Ns = count of n ≤ N with only small prime divisors. Use floor(N/p_i) bounds to show Nb < N/2 and bound Ns ≤ 2^k√N; choose N large (2^{2k+2}) to force Nb + Ns < N, contradiction, thus sum diverges. This is a template: split by size and count multiplicities carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of binomial-coefficient estimates and prime-factor products (Erdős approach to Bertrand's postulate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate central binomial coefficients and relate them to products over primes to infer existence of primes in (n,2n].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy steps: (1) handle small n by Landau's trick (a finite list of primes each < twice previous); (2) prove product_{p ≤ x} p ≤ 4^{x-1}; (3) apply Legendre's theorem to control multiplicities of primes dividing (2n choose n) and deduce that primes in (2n/3, n] do not divide (2n choose n); (4) combine bounds to contradict an assumption that no prime in (n,2n]. The text labels part of the argument a 'true Book Proof.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Landau's trick for finite verification
rubrics_metrics.description: To verify Bertrand's postulate for n up to some bound (e.g., n < 4000) it suffices to check a short sequence of primes where each is smaller than twice the previous one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example sequence given: 2,3,5,7,13,23,43,83,163,317,631,1259,2503,4001. Checking these 14 primes suffices to cover all n ≤ 4000 because every interval (n,2n] with n ≤ 4000 contains one of them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legendre's theorem for prime exponents in factorials
rubrics_metrics.description: The exponent of a prime p in n! equals sum_{k≥1} floor(n/p^k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to bound the multiplicity of primes in (2n)!/(n!)^2. The boxed statement and its proof are included; this is a standard counting tool to estimate valuations of factorials by primes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating factorials and binomial coefficients (Stirling, unimodality, simple bounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Stirling's formula and simple combinatorial bounds to estimate factorials and binomial coefficients; e.g., central binomial coefficient ≥ 2^{2n}/(2n) and ≤ 2^{2n}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appendix gives integral comparisons yielding n! bounds and Stirling's asymptotic n! ∼ sqrt(2πn)(n/e)^n, and simple binomial bounds: C(n,k) ≤ 2^n, middle binomial coefficients ≥ 2^n/ n, and tail bound C(n,k) ≤ n^k / 2^{k-1}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester's theorem as a tool to force large prime factors
rubrics_metrics.description: If n ≥ 2k then at least one of n, n-1, ..., n-k+1 has a prime divisor p > k (equivalently C(n,k) has a prime factor > k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a key ingredient in Erdős' analysis of when binomial coefficients can be perfect powers; the theorem ensures existence of large prime factors among consecutive integers and is invoked to derive lower bounds on n when C(n,k) = m^ℓ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square-free-part decomposition in Diophantine analysis of binomial coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Write each numerator factor n-j as a_j * m_j^ℓ where a_j is not divisible by any nontrivial ℓ-th power; analyze distinctness and prime divisors of the a_j's to derive contradictions when assuming C(n,k) = m^ℓ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Erdős' proof technique: show the a_j are distinct and must be exactly the integers 1..k in some order; use counting of prime exponents (via Legendre-type estimates) to deduce divisibility by k! and reach contradictions for ℓ ≥ 2 and k ≥ 4. The exposition highlights steps: distinctness of a_j, bounding prime exponents, and final combinatorial contradiction.
